name: Yusuf Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Hollis Farm, about seven hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, for the Hollis family. Right now, in November, it's mostly drilling the last of the winter wheat, carting grain from the store to lorries, and fixing whatever broke during harvest. I start at seven, get my jobs from Martin in the yard, and most days I'm in the tractor cab or up a ladder at the grain dryer until it's dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being out on my own in the cab when the light comes up over the field, honestly, nobody bothering me. What wears me out is harvest, when you're on the grain trailer fourteen hours a day for five weeks and you stop seeing your girlfriend except asleep. Amira says she shares a house with a smell of diesel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You've been there how long, and how did you start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Four years. I left school, did warehouse work, then my uncle knew Pete, who's been head tractor driver at Hollis for thirty years, and Pete got me in. I'm still learning, to be honest. Pete still does the drilling on the good fields because I've got a habit of leaving gaps on the headlands, the turning strips at the end of the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a better search engine, so what. Martin's son already looks up spray rates on his phone. It doesn't change who drives the trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing for me. I don't use these AI things and I wouldn't start just because they got a bit better. My job is diesel and grain dust, not typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Pay off the last bit of the car loan, keep putting about a hundred a month away, maybe do my sprayer licence if Martin pays for the course. Nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like hearing they've made a better kettle. Good for whoever wants one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about four months of money saved. What's that for, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's for the van dying or Amira's hours being cut at the vet's reception. It's not a house deposit, no chance, not on what I earn. Rent on Mill Lane went up forty a month in spring and that hurt more than any computer could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent hurt more than any computer could. Tell me about that letter.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It came in an envelope under the door in March, very polite, three lines. Forty more a month, from April. I read it out to Amira and she just said, well, that's the cinema gone, and she was right.

S0.say: I'd tell people it's a better search engine and nothing more. Martin's son looks up spray rates on his phone already, and it doesn't change who drives the trailer.
S0.think: I really think it means nothing for me, because my work is diesel and grain dust, not typing. I don't use AI and wouldn't start just because it got a bit better.
S0.do: Keeps going as now: pays off the last of his car loan and saves about a hundred a month. Asks Martin to pay for his sprayer licence course.
S0.feel: Calm. He compares it to news of a better kettle.
S0.quote: It's like hearing they've made a better kettle. Good for whoever wants one.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf's real money pressure is rent, not technology. He keeps steering back to landlords and the vet's hours, which suggests the big worries in his life are already there before any scenario starts. He was relaxed and a bit amused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story, companies using it as an excuse to squeeze people. If they hire fewer beginners, that's a choice bosses make, not the computer. I'd say it on the union group chat, and probably at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the beginner, aren't I. Four years in and Pete still won't let me drill the good fields. If Martin's son can get the drill to steer itself perfectly, there's no reason to keep a beginner who leaves gaps on the headlands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the jobs that aren't on a screen, that's all I can think of. Ask Pete to teach me the dryer properly, maybe the welding. Keep the four months saved and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not losing sleep, but it's there, like a noise in the engine you keep hearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the drill steering itself. Is that already happening on Hollis Farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. The new drill has GPS steering, a satellite thing that keeps the lines straight, and Martin's son set it up last year. I still turn it off sometimes because I don't trust it near the hedge. Pete laughs at me for that, but he trusts it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the farm would you worry about most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me first, then Pete, oddly. He's fifty-eight and the steering does what used to make him special, those dead straight lines. But Martin would never let Pete go, they've known each other since school.

S1.say: I'd say companies are using AI as an excuse to squeeze people, and hiring fewer beginners is a choice bosses make. I'd say it on the union group chat and at the pub.
S1.think: Just between us, I'm the beginner whose job is easiest to cut. If the drill steers itself perfectly, there's little reason to keep someone who still leaves gaps on the headlands.
S1.do: Asks Pete to teach him the grain dryer and welding so he's useful off-screen. Keeps his four months of savings untouched as a buffer.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in an engine he keeps hearing.
S1.quote: If Martin's son can get the drill to steer itself perfectly, there's no reason to keep a beginner who leaves gaps on the headlands.
S1.fieldNote: His public line blames bosses, but his private worry is his own skill gap. He turns the GPS steering off near hedges, which is a small, telling act of distrust. He's honest about being below average, which I didn't expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say look, it's the office people's turn now, and maybe they'll finally want a union. I'd share stuff online about the government protecting jobs. I'd be on the side of the people losing them, even the ones who looked down on farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it doesn't touch my job much. Grain still needs carting. But my sister does payroll at the council in town and she'd be the first to go, and then my mum leans on me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to join a union now, before anything happens. I'd keep the savings for her if she needed a month's rent. And I'd stop arguing online and go to an actual meeting, the farm workers' branch meets in the back room of the Plough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit guilty, if I'm honest, that I'm safe and she isn't. And angry on her behalf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd give your sister a month's rent. Would Amira be okay with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd argue about it, she'd say it's our buffer. But my sister helped me when I was nineteen and had nothing. You don't keep score with family, you just don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say at that meeting in the Plough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait for it to reach us. Last time the dairy down the road shut, nobody did anything until the workers were already gone. I'm not a speech person, though, I'd probably just say that and sit down.

S2.say: I'd say it's the office workers' turn and maybe they'll want a union now. I'd share posts about protecting jobs and stand with people losing them.
S2.think: I really think it barely touches me, since grain still needs carting. My worry is my sister, who does council payroll and would be first to go.
S2.do: Tells his sister to join a union straight away and sets aside a month's rent for her. Starts going to the farm workers' branch meetings in the back room of the Plough.
S2.feel: Guilty that he's safe while his sister isn't, and angry for her.
S2.quote: You don't keep score with family, you just don't.
S2.fieldNote: His concern moves sideways to his sister rather than himself. Family loyalty would beat his partner's wish to protect their buffer. His progressive views show up as action: he'd go to a real meeting, not just post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains belong to everyone, not to whoever owns the computers. If share prices boom while people lose jobs, tax it. I'd march if there was a march, I'm not shy about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it really means for me is the house thing. If house prices boom, I'm renting forever, and the landlord on Mill Lane puts the rent up again. My job's fine, physical jobs are fine, but fine doesn't buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Amira and do the sums properly for once, on paper. Probably look for a tied cottage, a house that comes with the job, even if it means moving farms. I'd ask Martin straight if he'd let us have the empty cottage by the grain store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Safe at work but squeezed at home, which is a strange feeling. Like being on a boat that's fine but the harbour's moving away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Martin when you asked about the cottage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've been here four years, I'm not going anywhere, and I'd rather pay you than a stranger. He'd probably say he needs it for a harvest worker. Then I'd know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tied cottage doesn't come, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we keep renting and I stop pretending we'll buy. Maybe we'd move further out, past the bypass, where it's cheaper and I drive longer. Amira won't like that, her mum's in town.

S3.say: I'd say the gains belong to everyone and booming share prices should be taxed. I'd march if there was a march and I wouldn't be shy about it.
S3.think: My job is safe, but booming house prices mean I'll rent forever while the landlord raises the rent. Fine at work doesn't buy a house.
S3.do: Sits down with Amira to do their sums properly on paper. Asks Martin directly for the empty cottage by the grain store, and looks at tied cottages on other farms if he says no.
S3.feel: Anxious: safe at work but squeezed at home.
S3.quote: Safe at work but squeezed at home, which is a strange feeling. Like being on a boat that's fine but the harbour's moving away.
S3.fieldNote: The threat here is housing, not his job, and he sees that clearly. He's resistant to new tech but would happily move farms for a cottage, so his caution is about technology, not change in general. The harbour line came out unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody protects workers, and I'd say it loudly. Farms are already the place with the fewest rules. I'd be telling everyone to join the union before the robots turn up, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one. I'm the cheapest thing on the farm to replace and the worst at the job. Martin's a decent man but he's not running a charity, and a robot doesn't leave gaps on the headlands or need harvest overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Pete what he's going to do, because whatever he does, I'll follow. I'd keep every bit of the savings and stop the hundred a month going anywhere fun. I'd look at lorry driving, because someone has to drive the grain lorries, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Proper stomach-ache alarmed. I don't know what I'd be if I wasn't on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amira the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're okay for four months, which is true, and then I'd go out and sit in the van for a bit. She'd come out with tea. She always knows when I'm in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would you learn to run the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was that or nothing, yes, I'd have to. I'd hate it and I'd be slow, like I am with the GPS. But I'd rather be the man fixing the robot in the field than the man at home watching it.

S4.say: I'd say loudly that this is what happens when nobody protects workers. I'd tell everyone to join the union before the robots arrive, not after.
S4.think: This is the one that really scares me. I'm the cheapest and worst on the farm to replace, and a robot doesn't leave gaps or need harvest overtime.
S4.do: Asks Pete about his plans and follows his lead. Freezes all spending, keeps the full four months of savings, and looks at lorry driving as a fallback.
S4.feel: Alarmed, with a real stomach-ache. He doesn't know who he'd be off a farm.
S4.quote: I'm the cheapest thing on the farm to replace and the worst at the job.
S4.fieldNote: This is where his calm broke. He's frank that he'd lose out to a robot before Pete would, and his instinct is to follow an older colleague rather than plan alone. The van-and-tea story showed a quiet, steady relationship under the worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, obviously. What would help is someone having to keep people like me on, or retrain us properly, paid, not a website course. And a union that's actually in the room when Martin buys the machine, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about rent, and that's what keeps me up now, today, without any robot. And maybe ask Pete. He's got thirty years and no plan B either, he just doesn't say it.

headlineQuote: I'm the cheapest thing on the farm to replace and the worst at the job.
portrait: Yusuf is 27, four years into a junior job on a 700-hectare grain and oilseed farm, and frank that he's still learning. He doesn't use AI and distrusts even the farm's GPS steering, but his left-leaning, pro-union views make him angry on behalf of others, especially his sister in council payroll. Through the first three pictures his real worry is rent and never owning a house. The robot picture breaks his calm: he sees himself as the first person to go and would follow his older colleague Pete's lead.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because he's the cheapest and least skilled worker on the farm and would be replaced first.
whatWouldHelp: Paid, proper retraining and a rule that employers keep or retrain workers, with a union present when the farm buys new machines.
